tagline: Working waterfronts, blueberry barrens and a striped light beside Quoddy Narrows.
intro: The Bold Coast National Scenic Byway runs 147 miles through coastal Washington County, from Milbridge to Calais. The drive connects fishing villages, blueberry barrens and riverside towns; beyond Cutler, the shores meet the rise and fall of the Bay of Fundy. DownEast Acadia Regional Tourism presents the national byway as a way to experience the region’s scenery, culture, wildlife and recreation, with working waterfronts central to its account. At Jonesport, the road reaches a peninsula between Chandler Bay, Wohoa Bay and the tidal Indian River, with islands offshore.

The ports along this corridor grew through connections across the water. Jonesport developed fishing and boatbuilding industries, while Eastport’s sardine fishery brought canneries along its shoreline. Those journeys needed navigational aids: a lighthouse was built at West Quoddy Head in 1808 to guide ships through Quoddy Narrows, and the present striped tower followed in 1858.

Begin on US 1 at Milbridge, then take in Jonesport before continuing to Machias. From East Machias, Route 191 leads through Cutler and past coves toward Route 189 in Lubec. West Quoddy Head lies southeast of Lubec; Eastport follows farther along the journey, before the finish inland at Calais on the tidal St. Croix River.

moments.title: Burnham Tavern, Machias
moments.text: Job Burnham’s 1770 tavern served both the planning of a battle and the care of its casualties. Local militia met here before the 1775 Battle of Machias, when townspeople captured the British armed vessel Margaretta. Afterward, wounded people from both sides were treated in the building. The wood-frame tavern has a gambrel roof, a large central chimney and a band of second-floor windows. Inside, a staircase branches left and right to give separate access to the upstairs bedrooms. Parlors occupy either side of the chimney, and a large kitchen fireplace fills much of the western half.
moments.notice: The gambrel roof includes a band of second-floor windows.

moments.title: West Quoddy Head Light
moments.text: The red-and-white tower at West Quoddy Head dates to 1858, fifty years after the first lighthouse was built here. Its purpose was to guide ships through Quoddy Narrows, the strait between Lubec and Canada’s Campobello Island. That passage leads into Passamaquoddy Bay and toward harbors on the St. Croix River. The circular brick tower stands 49 feet tall, with alternating horizontal stripes. West Quoddy Head is the easternmost point of the contiguous United States; the precise point lies on rocks extending east from the shore. The station also includes the former keeper’s quarters, a service building and an oil house.
moments.notice: Horizontal red and white stripes wrap the circular brick tower.

moments.title: Eastport
moments.text: A causeway connects the mainland with Moose Island, Eastport’s principal island. The harbor’s tides of about 25 feet kept it ice-free year round, and its shoreline filled with sardine canneries as that fishery grew. By 1886, thirteen factories operated day and night during the season. The fishing industry later declined and residents moved away; the city went bankrupt in 1937. DownEast Acadia’s tourism office describes the present Eastport as both a fishing port and an artist community, joining the waterfront’s working role to its arts life. Moose Island lies between Cobscook Bay to the west and Passamaquoddy Bay to the east.
